messages.subject: confidence interval for condition means from lmer
messages.subject_clean: confidence interval for condition means from lmer
messages.body_plain:
Hello everybody,

 

I apologize if this is a duplicate, but I could not find anything recent
about this.

 

With more and more journals asking for Confidence Intervals,
the question rises (again) how to calculate them for data with 
mixed random effects from an lmer model.

 

There is lots to find on CIs for model parameters, but this is not what I
want,
I want a CI for condition means in a 2x2 design.

 

Naively, I could think of using the residuals in each cell, and calculate
their standard deviation,

but then what would be the right N to get to a standard error?

 

Or would you find the following work around acceptable:

 

Aggregate to the subject and item level,
and then use the method by Morey (2008, see below) to calculate a CI
separately

for the subject- and item-aggregated data sets, and then use the outer
margins of those two CIs?

 

Kind regards,

Holger

 

 

Morey, R. D. (2008). Confidence intervals from normalized data: A correction
to Cousineau. In Tutorials in Quantitative Methods for Psychology , 4 (pp.
61-64).

 

 

-                      - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
- - - - - - -

messages.body_plain:
The "effects" package gives a simple way to calculate CIs for condition
means. For example:

> library(effects)

> library(languageR)

> m <- lmer(RTlexdec ~ WordCategory*AgeSubject + (1| Word), english)

> as.data.frame(effect("WordCategory:AgeSubject", m))

  WordCategory AgeSubject      fit          se    lower    upper

1            N        old 6.664176 0.002820814 6.658646 6.669706

2            V        old 6.656649 0.003619112 6.649554 6.663744

3            N      young 6.443781 0.002820814 6.438251 6.449311
4            V      young 6.432612 0.003619112 6.425517 6.439708

I think "lsmeans" package can also do this, though I'm less familiar with
it. I'm not sure what algorithm(s) they use, but there is some info here:
http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/117641/how-trustworthy-are-the-confidence-intervals-for-lmer-objects-through-effects-pa

Best,
Dan

messages.body_plain:
One option is to use parametric bootstrapping.


1. After you've fitted your lmer model, generate a data frame containing the cells you're interested in, e.g.:


cells <- expand.grid(ConditionAB = c("A", "B"),

ConditionCD = c("C", "D"))


2. If you have any covariates you want to fix at typical values (e.g., means, medians, mode, what have you), you can add them, too, e.g.:


cells$CovariateA <- mean(data$CovariateA)


3. Add the cell means predicted by the model:


cells$Prediction <- predict(mod.mer, cells, re.form = NA)


4.  Create a matrix to be filled with bootstrapped predictions:


bs.predictions <- matrix(ncol = 1000, nrow = nrow(cells))


5. Duplicate 'cells'


bs.cells <- cells


6.


# Loop: Simulate new data from model, refit model on new data,
# get predictions, write predictions to bs.predictions, and do this 1000 times.
for (i in 1:1000) {
  # Simulate new data on the basis of mod.f2
  dat$Simulated <- unlist(simulate(mod.mer))

  # Fit mod.mer to simulated data
  bs.mod <- ## write your model here, but use "Simulated" as the outcome variable

  # Generate predictions on the basis of bs.mod
  predictions <- predict(bs.mod, bs.cells, re.form = NA)

  # Add these predictions to a new column in bs.predictions
  bs.predictions[, i] <- predictions
}


7. Find the percentiles you're interested in and add them to cells. For a 95% CI: 0.025 and 0.975.


cells$LoCI <- apply(bs.predictions, 1,  quantile, probs = 0.025)
cells$HiCI <- apply(bs.predictions, 1,  quantile, probs = 0.975)


8. [cells$LoCI, cells$HiCI] contains 95% CIs for the cell means.



HTH,

Jan

Hello everybody,

I apologize if this is a duplicate, but I could not find anything recent about this.

With more and more journals asking for Confidence Intervals,
the question rises (again) how to calculate them for data with
mixed random effects from an lmer model.

There is lots to find on CIs for model parameters, but this is not what I want,
I want a CI for condition means in a 2x2 design.

Naively, I could think of using the residuals in each cell, and calculate their standard deviation,
but then what would be the right N to get to a standard error?

Or would you find the following work around acceptable:

Aggregate to the subject and item level,
and then use the method by Morey (2008, see below) to calculate a CI separately
for the subject- and item-aggregated data sets, and then use the outer margins of those two CIs?

Kind regards,
Holger




Morey, R. D. (2008). Confidence intervals from normalized data: A correction to Cousineau. In Tutorials in Quantitative Methods for Psychology , 4 (pp. 61-64).

> On 3 Mar 2017, at 20:55, Dan Mirman <dan-uZj4hkX1dquEi8DpZVb4nw at public.gmane.org <mailto:dan at danmirman.org>> wrote:
> 
> I think "lsmeans" package can also do this, 

And will give virtually identical results (here, with adjusted covariance calculations disabled):
library(lmeans)
library(effects)
library(languageR)

> m <- lmer(RTlexdec ~ WordCategory*AgeSubject + (1|Word), english)

> as.data.frame(effect("WordCategory:AgeSubject", m))
  WordCategory AgeSubject      fit          se    lower    upper
1            N        old 6.664176 0.002820814 6.658646 6.669706
2            V        old 6.656649 0.003619112 6.649554 6.663744
3            N      young 6.443781 0.002820814 6.438251 6.449311
4            V      young 6.432612 0.003619112 6.425517 6.439708

> eng.lsm <- lsmeans(m, "WordCategory", by="AgeSubject")
> eng.lsm
AgeSubject = old:
 WordCategory   lsmean          SE df asymp.LCL asymp.UCL
 N            6.664176 0.002820814 NA  6.658647  6.669704
 V            6.656649 0.003619112 NA  6.649556  6.663742

AgeSubject = young:
 WordCategory   lsmean          SE df asymp.LCL asymp.UCL
 N            6.443781 0.002820814 NA  6.438252  6.449310
 V            6.432612 0.003619112 NA  6.425519  6.439706

Confidence level used: 0.95 

Behind the scenes, lsmeans relies the PBmodcomp function from the pbkrtest package, which uses parametric bootstrap. cf. Jan’s roll-your-own method:
> cells
  AgeSubject WordCategory Prediction     LoCI     HiCI
1        old            N   6.664176 6.659008 6.669882
2      young            N   6.443781 6.438246 6.449022
3        old            V   6.656649 6.649747 6.663679
4      young            V   6.432612 6.425705 6.439766
